column2: On the authority of the Commander of the Believers, Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (Allah the Exalted bless him and his family and grant them peace) say:

“Actions are only by intentions, and every person shall have only what he intended. So whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for some worldly gain he would attain, or a woman he would marry, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated.”

Reported by the two imams of the hadith scholars, Abū ʿAbdillāh Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mughīrah ibn Bardizbah al-Bukhārī and Abū al-Ḥusayn Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj ibn Muslim al-Qushayrī al-Naysābūrī, in their two Ṣaḥīḥs, which are the most authentic of compiled books.
Innamā (“only”): for restriction, which is affirming the ruling for what is mentioned and negating it for everything else.
Al-aʿmāl (“actions”): those prescribed by the Sharīʿah that require an intention.
Bi-l-niyyāt (“by intentions”): with the yāʾ doubled or light; the plural of niyyah, which is the resolve of the heart.
“And every person shall have only what he intended”: whoever intends something obtains nothing other than it.
“So whoever's emigration was”: his moving from the land of shirk to the land of Islam.
“To Allah and His Messenger”: his aim in emigrating being obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to His Messenger ﷺ.
“His emigration is to Allah and His Messenger”: in reward and recompense.

Li-dunyā (“for some worldly gain”): with ḍammah or kasrah on the dāl, from dunuww, meaning nearness. It is so called because it comes before the other life, or because it is near to passing away. It is what is on the earth, together with the air and the atmosphere, before the Hour is established.
It has been said that what is meant by it here is wealth, as indicated by a woman being mentioned alongside it.
Yuṣībuhā (“he would attain it”): he would obtain it.
The printed gloss reads يحصيها (“count it”), evidently a misprint for يحصلها (“obtain it”), the gloss given in al-Sharḥ al-Mūjaz; the translation follows the intended reading.
Yankiḥuhā (“he would marry her”): he would take her as a wife.
“His emigration is to that for which he emigrated”: whatever it may be. The first is a merchant and the second a suitor.
Encouragement to sincerity, for Allah accepts only a deed that is correct and by which His Face is sought.
For this reason, the scholars considered it recommended to open written works with this hadith, to alert the student to correcting his intention.

Acts by which one draws near to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, if done by a legally responsible person (mukallaf) out of habit, do not earn reward merely for being done, even if they are valid, until he intends by them to draw near to Allah.
The virtue of emigrating to Allah and His Messenger.

Emigration in Islam took place in two forms. The first: moving from a land of fear to a land of safety, as in the two emigrations to Abyssinia and the beginning of the emigration from Makkah to Madīnah.
The second: emigrating from the land of disbelief to the land of faith, after the Prophet ﷺ had settled in Madīnah and those Muslims who were able emigrated to him.
At that time, emigration was specifically moving to Madīnah, until Makkah was conquered and that specificity ended.
The general obligation to move from the land of disbelief to the land of Islam remained for whoever is able to do so.
